messages.subject: Benefits of using logistic regression (replicates)
parts:
Hello,

I have been reading about how to deal with replicates when preforming differential analysis. And here is what I am understanding:

No replicates:
It is clear that when no replicates are available, the best we can do is a Fischer's exact test ( or a Chi square test).

Replicates:
- When replicates are available, we can choose to be very stringent (i.e  sensitive to small differences) by pooling replicates to force the Fischer's exact test.
- If replicates are kept separated, my understanding (discussed here https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/methylkit_discussion/regression/methylkit_discussion/eLs44aJdIfU/RiR6bIbOrP8J ) is that the counts for Cs (methylated) and Ts (unmethylated) are summed across regions and a logistic regression is performed between treatment and control groups.

If keeping replicates separated is meant to access and account for biological variability, I was wondering if this is what is done using logistic regression. Does it take into account this variability?

If we only sum the count across replicates, doesn't that mimic pooling replicates? if that's the case, what is the benefit of keeping replicates separated and using logistic regression? (as opposed to pooling + Fischer's test)

Any input would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
